41.quote_or_event: “It will not behove me, during the life of my parents, to tear out my hair, and leaving the house to enter the state of houselessness.”
41.explanation: While still in the womb, Mahāvīra resolves not to renounce the household while his parents live, so that the future Jina himself first fulfils the householder's obligation to those who depend on him.
41.tie_back: Valluvar defines the true householder as the steady support of those who rely on him, and the Kalpa Sūtra has the greatest Jain renouncer defer his own vocation until that support is no longer needed.
41.source: Kalpa Sūtra, Life of Mahāvīra §94 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)
41._accuracy_note: Wording verified on wisdomlib's Jacobi text. A real Jain parallel for duty to dependants, but it concerns parents only, not the 'three' of the Kural's commentators, and the passage frames household duty as a stage before renunciation.

42.quote_or_event: “Yathavat atithau sadhau dine cha pratipatti-krt : Diligent in succoring the ascetics, the righteous and the needy.”
42.explanation: Hemacandra counts care for ascetics and the destitute among the defining qualities of a good Jain layman, and the lay vow of atithi-saṃvibhāga commits the householder to eat only after feeding mendicants.
42.tie_back: Two of the Kural's three dependants, those who have renounced and those who have nothing to eat, are exactly the people Jain lay ethics charges the householder to support.
42.source: Hemacandra, Yogaśāstra 1.47–56 (the thirty-five householder qualities, no. 19), English as given in V. A. Sangave, Ethics of Jainism
42._accuracy_note: The English is Sangave's rendering as published on jainworld.com, not a direct translation of the Sanskrit verse. Jain doctrine does not accept rites that feed or benefit the dead, so the Kural's third dependant (iṟantār) has no Jain counterpart.

43.quote_or_event: “The six daily activities or duties of householders are : worship of God, worship of the preceptor, study of scriptures, practice of self control, practice of austerities, and giving gifts.”
43.explanation: A widely cited Sanskrit verse (devapūjā gurūpāstiḥ svādhyāyaḥ saṃyamas tapaḥ / dānaṃ ceti gṛhasthānāṃ ṣaṭ karmāṇi dine dine) gives the Jain householder a fixed list of daily duties.
43.tie_back: Jainism has its own list of the householder's daily duties that sits beside Valluvar's fivefold one, though the two lists are not the same.
43.source: Ṣaḍ-āvaśyaka verse for householders, as quoted and translated in V. A. Sangave, Ethics of Jainism (jainworld.com)
43._accuracy_note: Next-best match. The duties differ: 'God' here means the Jina, who receives nothing from offerings, and Jainism makes no offerings to ancestors (tenpulattār). Sangave does not name the verse's author.

44.quote_or_event: “Nyayasampannavibhavah : Possessed of honestly earned wealth.” … “Papabhiru : Apprehensive of sin.”
44.explanation: Hemacandra's list of the ideal layman's qualities opens with wealth earned by just means and soon adds fear of wrongdoing, putting ethical acquisition first among the householder's virtues.
44.tie_back: Valluvar's 'fearing blame' in earning is matched almost word for word by Hemacandra's first and third qualities, honest wealth and fear of sin, and the Jain duty of giving supplies the Kural's 'sharing what one eats'.
44.source: Hemacandra, Yogaśāstra 1.47–56 (the thirty-five householder qualities, nos. 1 and 3), English as given in V. A. Sangave, Ethics of Jainism
44._accuracy_note: A close fit for the Kural's first condition. The promise that the family line will never fail has no direct Jain equivalent, and the English is Sangave's rendering.

45.quote_or_event: In the Uvāsagadasāo the wealthy merchant Ānanda of Vāṇijyagrāma takes the twelve lay vows from Mahāvīra, and his wife Śivanandā goes to Mahāvīra and takes the same vows, so that the couple share a single discipline as householders.
45.explanation: The first and model story of the Jain lay canon shows a household whose love is joined to shared observance of the vows, with both husband and wife counted as members of the fourfold community.
45.tie_back: Valluvar says love joined with virtue is both the nature and the fruit of household life, and Ānanda and Śivanandā are the Jain canon's model of that union of affection and dharma in one home.
45.source: Uvāsagadasāo (Upāsakadaśāḥ) ch. 1, story of Ānanda (tr. A. F. R. Hoernlé, 1890); summary at jainworld.com
45._accuracy_note: The vow-taking by Ānanda and Śivanandā is confirmed on jainworld.com, but I could not read Hoernlé's text this session. The story is about vows, not marital love as such, so the fit is thematic.

46.quote_or_event: “Bark and skin (of a goat), nakedness, twisted hair, baldness--these (outward tokens) will not save a sinful ascetic. … A sinner, though he be a mendicant (friar), will not escape hell; but a pious man, whether monk or householder, ascends to heaven.”
46.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana denies that the outward marks of renunciation are worth anything in themselves: a virtuous householder reaches heaven just as a virtuous monk does.
46.tie_back: When the Kural asks what a virtuous householder would gain by taking the 'other path', the Jain sūtra answers in part: the ascetic's insignia gain nothing on their own.
46._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com. Jainism agrees about heavenly reward but still holds that final liberation needs full renunciation (5.20, 5.25), so it does not fully endorse the Kural's 'what more is there?'.

47.quote_or_event: When Gautama, Mahāvīra's chief disciple, doubted the lay votary Ānanda's claim to have attained avadhi-jñāna (clairvoyant knowledge), Mahāvīra told him Ānanda was right and that Gautama himself should ask forgiveness, and Gautama went back to the householder and apologised.
47.explanation: In the Uvāsagadasāo a disciplined householder reaches a degree of spiritual knowledge that the foremost monk had wrongly doubted, and the Jina publicly confirms the layman's standing.
47.tie_back: Valluvar places the true householder at the head of all who strive, and the story of Ānanda has Mahāvīra rank a householder's attainment above the senior monk's judgment.
47.source: Uvāsagadasāo (Upāsakadaśāḥ) ch. 1, story of Ānanda (tr. A. F. R. Hoernlé, 1890); retold in Jain Story Series, 'Anand Shravak'
47._accuracy_note: A well-attested canonical episode, confirmed this session only from a modern retelling. Ānanda had by then taken the advanced lay stages (pratimās), so he is an exceptional householder, not an ordinary one.

48.quote_or_event: “Some householders are superior to some monks in self-control; but the saints are superior to all householders in self-control.”
48.explanation: Mahāvīra's teaching admits that a disciplined householder can surpass a lax monk in self-restraint, while still ranking the true saints above every layman.
48.tie_back: The Kural says a virtuous household has more strength than the penance of ascetics, and the Uttarādhyayana grants the same point for some householders against some monks.
48._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim. The first half is a close parallel, but the second half keeps the Jain hierarchy, so the Jain claim is narrower than Valluvar's.

49.quote_or_event: “The householder, whose interior is illumined with Right Faith, follows the ‘path;’ but the ascetic involved in wrong beliefs is nowhere near it; for this reason the ‘enlightened’ householder is considered superior to an ascetic devoid of true faith.”
49.explanation: Samantabhadra holds that inner right faith, not the outward state of life, decides who is on the path to liberation, so an enlightened householder outranks a deluded ascetic.
49.tie_back: Valluvar calls household life virtue itself and accepts renunciation only where it is beyond reproach, and Samantabhadra likewise makes the ascetic's worth depend on his being sound within.
49.source: Samantabhadra, Ratnakaraṇḍa Śrāvakācāra v. 33 (gṛhastho mokṣamārgastho…), tr. Champat Rai Jain, 1917, pp. 18–19
49._accuracy_note: Verified against the archive.org OCR of Champat Rai Jain's 1917 translation. His edition does not number the verses, so 'v. 33' follows the standard Sanskrit numbering. His own note adds that as a rule the ascetic takes precedence.

50.quote_or_event: “When under such discipline he lives piously even as a householder, he will, on quitting flesh and bones, share the world of the Yakshas.”
50.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana promises a heavenly rebirth among the gods to a householder who keeps the lay rules and the fortnightly fast.
50.tie_back: Valluvar says the one who lives as life should be lived will be counted among the sky-dwelling gods, and the Jain sūtra gives the same reward to the pious householder.
50._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com. In Jainism heaven is still within saṃsāra and is not liberation, which is a real difference in framing from the Kural's climactic praise.
